name: Vocabulary Profile Analysis
description: Profiles vocabulary usage against frequency bands (K1-K20) to detect AI's tendency toward mid-frequency words (Nation, 2001).
mechanism:
This method profiles vocabulary usage against BNC/COCA frequency bands (K1–K20) to detect AI text, which clusters in mid-frequency ranges and avoids both very common colloquial words and rare specialized vocabulary:

1. **Frequency Band Classification**: Every content word in the text is mapped to its frequency band using Nation's (2001) BNC/COCA word family lists: K1 (most frequent 1,000 families), K2 (1,001–2,000), through K20 (19,001–20,000), plus off-list words (beyond K20 or proper nouns). The vocabulary profile (VP) records the percentage of tokens falling in each band. The VocabProfile/Compleat Lexical Tutor methodology (Cobb, 2000) is followed for consistent tokenization and lemmatization.

2. **AI Vocabulary Signature Detection**: AI-generated text exhibits a characteristic mid-frequency clustering: overuse of K3–K6 'educated vocabulary' (words like 'furthermore', 'significant', 'demonstrate', 'comprehensive') and underuse of K1 colloquialisms ('gonna', 'stuff', 'kinda') and K12+ specialized terms ('amortize', 'denouement', 'peristalsis'). The mid-frequency ratio (K3–K6 tokens / total content words) serves as the primary metric: AI text shows MFR ≈ 0.38 versus human text MFR ≈ 0.24. The off-list word ratio (OLR) provides complementary signal: human expert text OLR ≈ 0.08 versus AI OLR ≈ 0.03.

3. **Lexical Sophistication Indices**: Multiple indices from Crossley et al.'s (2011) TAALES system are computed: (a) word frequency (log BNC frequency, mean and SD), (b) word range (number of text types a word appears in), (c) academic word coverage (Coxhead's 2000 Academic Word List, 570 families), (d) contextual distinctiveness (how predictable a word is from its context). AI text shows higher Academic Word List coverage (12–18%) compared to human text of equivalent topic (7–11%), reflecting AI's tendency to deploy formal academic vocabulary regardless of register.

4. **Distribution Shape Analysis**: Beyond mean frequency, the shape of the vocabulary frequency distribution is analyzed. Human text follows a Zipfian distribution modified by genre and authorial style, with distinctive tail behavior in the rare-word region. AI text shows a truncated distribution — fewer extreme-frequency words in both directions — producing lower kurtosis (human κ ≈ 4.2 versus AI κ ≈ 2.8). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the text's frequency distribution and genre-specific human baselines provides a composite detection metric.
parameters:
Frequency lists: BNC/COCA K1–K20 (Nation 2001), 20,000 word families
AWL: Coxhead 2000, 570 word families
Mid-frequency ratio threshold: MFR > 0.32 indicates AI-typical
Lexical indices: TAALES (Crossley et al. 2011)
Minimum input: 200 tokens for reliable profiling
accuracy: 79–87% accuracy for AI detection via vocabulary profile. Mid-frequency ratio achieves AUC 0.83. Off-list word ratio alone separates with 74% accuracy. Combined vocabulary profile reaches 87% on academic and journalistic text. Lower (73%) on technical domains with naturally high specialized vocabulary.
source: Nation, I.S.P. (2001). Learning Vocabulary in Another Language. Cambridge University Press. • Crossley, S.A., Salsbury, T., & McNamara, D.S. (2011). 'Predicting Lexical Proficiency in Language Learner Texts Using Computational Indices.' Language Testing, 29(2). • Coxhead, A. (2000). 'A New Academic Word List.' TESOL Quarterly, 34(2).
useCase: Detects AI-generated text through its unnaturally compressed vocabulary range — effective for academic essays, journalism, and creative writing where human authors naturally deploy both colloquial and specialized vocabulary across the full frequency spectrum.
strengths:
• Based on established corpus linguistics methodology (Nation 2001)
• Mid-frequency clustering is a robust AI signature
• Frequency band analysis is fast and interpretable
• AWL coverage ratio captures formality mismatch
• Distribution shape analysis adds statistical rigor
limitations:
• ESL writers may show similar mid-frequency clustering
• Domain-specific text naturally has different frequency profiles
• Vocabulary profile varies significantly with text length
• AI models fine-tuned on domain corpora may show more natural profiles
• Proper noun handling requires careful pre-processing

references.title: Nation (2001) — Learning Vocabulary in Another Language, Cambridge University Press
Crossley, Salsbury & McNamara (2011) — Predicting Lexical Proficiency, Language Testing
